title: Command Injection Risks knowledge check

questions.prompt: Which topic is explicitly listed under “Command Injection Risks”?
options: Why evaluating constructed command strings is dangerous
questions.answer_key: Why evaluating constructed command strings is dangerous
questions.explanation: The supplied Bash.pdf curriculum lists “Why evaluating constructed command strings is dangerous” under lesson 131, “Command Injection Risks”. Review the topic in the lesson content to connect the term with its practical use.

questions.prompt: Which approach is the strongest default when applying “Command Injection Risks”?
options: Evaluate constructed user-controlled strings as shell commands to reduce parsing code.
Skip version checks because all common environments provide the same Bash features.
Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
Assume that a working happy-path example proves correctness for every input.
questions.answer_key: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls.
questions.explanation: Keep untrusted text as data and use least privilege with explicit side-effect controls. This approach keeps assumptions visible and makes results verifiable.

questions.prompt: Which practice best prevents a common reliability or maintenance error related to “Command Injection Risks”?
options: Assume the command behaves the same across all versions and operating systems.
Skip invalid inputs because the example uses trusted sample data.
Treat one successful output as proof that the workflow is safe in production.
Keep data separate from command syntax, validate access and paths, and avoid exposing credentials.
questions.answer_key: Keep data separate from command syntax, validate access and paths, and avoid exposing credentials.
questions.explanation: Keep data separate from command syntax, validate access and paths, and avoid exposing credentials. The appropriate checks depend on the target environment and should be reviewed before publishing a script.
